title_en: Accents, iota subscript, punctuation and typing
summary_en: The three accent marks and what to do with them for now; the iota subscript; Greek punctuation; and typing all of it.

grammar.md:
**Three marks, one job.** Almost every Greek word carries one accent on one of its last three syllables: the **acute** ά, the **grave** ὰ, or the **circumflex** ᾶ. In Ariston's Athens they marked a rise or fall of pitch, like a musical note. In this course the voice gives the accented syllable a little more weight, the way English stresses a syllable, and that is what you should do too: say θε-**ός**, **ἄν**-θρω-πος, ἀ-**νήρ**.

**Grave.** An acute on the last syllable turns into a grave when another word follows without a pause: καλός, but καλὸς ὁ ἀνήρ. Same word, same accent, different mark. Treat them as one.

**Circumflex.** Only on a long vowel or diphthong: ποῦ, τῷ, ἀγορᾷ. Say it like the acute for now.

**Typing.** Until Unit 4 the app accepts answers without accents; breathings always count (ὁ is not ὀ). Type what you can; check the model answer; over time the accents will come from what you read and hear.

**Iota subscript.** A tiny ι under a long vowel: ᾳ ῃ ῳ. It was once pronounced (*āi*, *ēi*, *ōi*) and by 400 BC was fading; we do not sound it, but it marks important endings: τῷ οἴκῳ, τῇ ἀγορᾷ. Learn to see it.

**Punctuation.** Full stop and comma as in English. The **semicolon ;** is the Greek **question mark**: τίς; 'who?'. The **raised dot ·** is a colon or semicolon: καλὸς ὁ ἀνήρ· καλὴ ἡ γυνή. Quotation is usually « ». Capitals for names only.

culture.title: School in Athens
culture.md: Athenian boys of Lysis's age went to a **grammatistes** to learn letters, then to a **kitharistes** for music and to the palaestra for wrestling. A famous red-figure cup by the painter Douris shows the whole curriculum: a boy reciting from a papyrus roll, another with a lyre, a third at a wax tablet, and a *paidagogos* (a slave who walked the boy to school) watching from a chair. The text on the roll is a line of epic verse. Girls like Elpis normally learned at home. The accent marks you have just met were not part of any of this: Lysis learned his letters, and the melody of the words, by ear.
